Super excited to be getting involved with the HR and employment law side of documents, drafting and advice at New Legal, run by the awesome Ian Greig MBA.

New Legal specialise in commercial and corporate law, including areas which, frankly, terrify me (I’m looking at you, shareholder agreements and IP!).

Ian’s vision is that New Legal are innovative, accessible and non-traditional. It’s in the name!

New Legal welcome clients that are happy to take a bit of risk when it comes to tricky decisions, while protecting the bits that matter.

And that’s my approach to HR and employment, so it all makes perfect sense!

If any business owners in my network needs this sort of documentation or advice then I can’t recommend Ian and the team highly enough.

Check out the website here: https://new-legal.com/

posts.fullText:
My personal Facebook account got hacked, then suspended, the hacker appealed the suspension and then Meta deleted the account. Just like that.

There is no way for me to appeal this (because it has already been appealed by the hacker!) and there is no way for me to speak to a human (because you need to be logged in to do that!).

I'd also like to add that 2FA was enabled, as were passkeys. Really scary that someone can bypass this (although FB do allow you to skip passkeys and use 2FA via email which defeats the whole point of passkeys?).

Anyone know of a human being that works at Meta?

I don't actually care, I only used it to binge watch reels of people cleaning really dirty floors but it's not the point!

HR On Call Ltd and Rocket Digital Ltd are now Cyber Essentials qualified.

Honestly... seems like a bit of a waste of time to me - I didn't have to change anything to be compliant but I easily could have made everything up just to get the certificate.

I don't need pay £300 to ensure good data security and compliance for my clients - it's just part of the package and super important.

posts.fullText:
Yesterday, an article I’d written with the Telegraph was published. It was about why companies need HR. It was opinion. The comments from readers were absolutely mind blowing.

Nasty. Personal. Deeply unkind. Very unnecessary. Occasionally supportive.

And also really rude about my cat, and implying that a cat on my desk (of my home office…) meant something about me. I actually don’t know what it apparently means, other than I like cats and I work from home.

But I’ve also had comments like these on LinkedIn posts and comments too.

I don’t post any opinionated comments on other people’s posts now because it turns into people using the 😂 as their comment or reaction in response or a nasty comment.

It’s got me thinking.

None of the comments would have been made to my face.

So why is it ok to say it to me (or anyone) from behind a keyboard?

Why do we tolerate this sort of behaviour online?

And why would anyone find it acceptable to do this to someone that they don’t even know?

Anyway. I’m genuinely worried that society is collapsing again and that the end of humankind will be coming soon, and we’ll be replaced by AI!

At least those commenters will have their wish and be free from evil HR 😂

For the record, I’m ok with people writing what they did. Has no reflection on me, only on them!

Although I am still smarting a bit from being called “woke” and a “far-left extremist” 😅

The Telegraph have published the article that I wrote with them, which was an attempt to defend HR following the story about how Bolt ditched its entire HR team.

Colleagues, I tried my best. I hope that I did you proud.

But the comments that readers have left... absolutely savage (although I'm sure most of them didn't actually read what I wrote?).

Anyway. I won't be trying to publicly defend us all again. Or let myself read any more of these nasty comments! 😭

Photo credit: the very kind Jim Wileman who put me at ease and got flirted with by my cat Luna, who gatecrashed the party and got included.

Article here: https://lnkd.in/gbYKbA6a

posts.fullText:
Tipping law is changing again 🫠

You might already know that since October 2024, employers have had to pass on all tips to workers in full, with no unfair deductions. That’s the Employment (Allocation of Tips) Act 2023 and it isn’t going anywhere.

What’s new comes from the Employment Rights Act 2025.

🚀Consult before you write the policy.

Before an employer produces its first written tipping policy, it has to consult workers about it. Through a trade union or elected reps if there are any, or directly with staff if there aren’t.

🚀The duty is the same every time you review it.

Every time the policy is substantively reviewed, that consultation happens again. It isn’t a one off box to tick when the policy is born.

🚀There will be a three year review clock, and it may already be ticking.

Every written tipping policy has to be formally reviewed at least once every three years. For clients who already have a policy, that clock runs from when the policy was first put in place, not from whenever the new law lands. Some are closer to a mandatory review than they think.

There’s also a new duty to share an anonymised written summary of what staff said in the consultation, so it can’t just happen behind closed doors.

This was expected to land in October 2026. The draft revised Code of Practice was published in July, then withdrawn without explanation, then reissued for a fresh consultation that closes 29 September 2026. Implementation is now expected “by the end of 2026”, not a fixed date.

We’re going to need a policy on how we’ll write TRONC policies at this rate 🙄

I’m frustrated for hospitality employers who already are struggling.

The HR Vault does have a TRONC toolkit to help with current rules and it’ll be updated as and when we get more guidance and a confirmed Code of Practice.

Full article on the TRONC updates plus links to the draft guidance here: https://lnkd.in/gsvsUXSj
